summary: H.R. 10184, the Consumer Financial Protection Accountability and Reform Act of 2026, makes structural and procedural changes to the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection. The bill alters how the Bureau is funded, revises supervisory thresholds, modifies requirements for issuing rules and conducting cost-benefit analyses, places new limits on enforcement actions, establishes safe harbors and legal frameworks for specific credit and earned wage access products, and sets new standards for consumer complaint processing and interagency coordination.

affected_groups.effect: Faces altered funding mechanisms, mandatory cost-benefit analysis frameworks, enhanced OMB oversight of existing rules, procedural limits on defining abusive acts, and new coordination requirements with prudential regulators.

Institutions with assets under $30,000,000,000 are moved out of direct Bureau supervision unless an election or exception applies, and qualifying entities gain access to safe harbors for small-dollar credit products.
affected_groups.group: Banks, Savings Associations, and Credit Unions

affected_groups.effect: Subject to federal standards regarding fee disclosures, no-cost transfer options, prohibitions on late fees or credit reporting, and preemption of state laws treating these services as credit or loans.

Required to provide direct notice to covered entities 60 days prior and attest under penalty of perjury when submitting complaints to the Bureau, while gaining standardized disclosures for financial products and earned wage access.
Afforded enhanced consideration in regulatory flexibility analyses and improved loan privacy protections under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act.

key_provisions: Brings the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection into the regular congressional appropriations process.
Requires the Office of Management and Budget Director to review major rules or orders issued by the Bureau not later than 8 years after compliance is required, and non-major rules within 10 years.
Establishes a safe harbor for insured depository institutions and credit unions offering small-dollar credit products of $3,500 or less that meet specific structural and underwriting requirements.

Raises the asset threshold for bank, savings association, and credit union supervision by the Bureau from $10,000,000,000 to $30,000,000,000, and allows qualifying institutions to make a supervisory election.
Establishes comprehensive federal requirements, disclosure rules, and consumer protections for earned wage access services, preventing them from being treated as loans or credit under federal law.

Imposes strict requirements for consumer complaints submitted to the Bureau, including an attestation under penalty of perjury that the consumer directly informed the covered person of the issue at least 60 days prior.
Requires the President to appoint an Inspector General specifically for the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection, subject to Senate confirmation.

summary_detail.plain_summary: H.R. 10184, the Consumer Financial Protection Accountability and Reform Act of 2026, makes structural and procedural changes to the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection. The bill alters how the Bureau is funded, revises supervisory thresholds, modifies requirements for issuing rules and conducting cost-benefit analyses, places new limits on enforcement actions, establishes safe harbors and legal frameworks for specific credit and earned wage access products, and sets new standards for consumer complaint processing and interagency coordination.
summary_detail.significance: The bill implements sweeping administrative, structural, and legal restrictions on the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection, shifting its oversight methods, changing funding structures, establishing distinct product safe harbors, and altering federal engagement with financial institutions and consumer financial service providers.
